title: Capstone: Arguing an Interpretation from Text and Commentary
bigQuestion: How do you build an honest argument about what a passage of the Tanakh does and how its readers have read it?

story.title: One Verse, Four Voices, Two Chairs
story.kicker: Two students take one verse of Genesis 22, open four commentaries, and end not with a winner but with a better question.
paragraphs: Dev and Rosa have the same passage for their capstone: Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac, which Jewish tradition calls the Akedah. They have the same verse, too, 22:2, where God tells Abraham, "Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac." Their teacher has set the two of them across a table with a stack of books between them and one rule. Nobody may say "I feel like" without pointing to a line.

Rosa starts with the plain sense. The verse piles up four descriptions before it says the name: son, only son, the one you love, Isaac. "Why not just say Isaac?" she asks. Dev opens Rashi. Rashi, quoting the Talmud, turns the verse into a conversation: Abraham says he has two sons; God says the only one; Abraham says each is the only son of his mother; God says the one you love; Abraham says he loves them both; and only then, Isaac. Rosa laughs. "So Rashi thinks the slowness is Abraham stalling, or God being gentle?"

Dev finds Ibn Ezra, who is not interested in the drama. He wants to know how old Isaac was. A midrash says thirty-seven, since Sarah dies in the next chapter; Ibn Ezra objects that a grown man carried to the altar would be the real hero, and the text would have said so. He guesses Isaac was around thirteen. Rosa reads Ramban on the word "tested": a test, Ramban says, is for the sake of the one tested, to turn what is possible into what is done. Then she reads a page of Erich Auerbach, who says the whole scene is "fraught with background," silent about everything except what is needed.

By the end of the period they have not agreed on what the verse means. But they have agreed on what it does: it slows the reader down at the moment the command lands. Rosa's thesis is that the four-step naming is the text's way of making the reader feel the weight. Dev's is that the commentators each fill the same silence with what they most need, a dialogue, a fact, a purpose. Their teacher writes on the board the question they both landed on: what is a reader supposed to do with a text that refuses to explain itself?
story.think: Dev and Rosa never decided who was right. What did they produce instead, and why might that be worth more in a class about how a text has been read?

lessons.title: A Passage and a Question
lessons.mainIdea: A good capstone starts with a short passage you can quote in full and one question the passage itself raises.
reading: The capstone asks you to do what this course has watched others do for two thousand years: read a passage closely, hear its readers, and make a claim. The first move is choosing well. A passage should be short enough to quote in full, usually three to fifteen verses, and rich enough to have a history of readers. Genesis 22, Genesis 4:1 to 16, Exodus 3:1 to 15, Jonah 4, Ruth 1, Psalm 22 and Isaiah 6 all work. A whole book does not. A single word can, if it sits in a verse readers have argued about, like *oved* in Deuteronomy 26:5.

The second move is a question the text raises, not one you bring to it. "Is God fair?" is a question you brought. "Why does Genesis 22:2 give four descriptions of Isaac before his name?" is a question the verse raises, because a plain reader notices the pile-up. Test a question by asking whether two careful readers could answer it differently by pointing at the text. If only one answer is possible, the question is too small. If no line in the passage helps, it is too big.

Keep the question descriptive and the stance neutral, as the whole course has. You are not being asked whether the Tanakh is true, whether God exists or whether Abraham did right. You are asked what the text does with its words and how Jewish readers, and where relevant Christian and academic readers, have read it. That frame is not a limit on thinking. It is what makes a public-school classroom able to study a sacred text at all, and it is what lets people who disagree about God agree about a verb.

words.d: a final project that gathers the skills of a course into one piece of work
a short stretch of text, usually a few verses, chosen for close study
a question about what a text says or does, rather than whether it is true

look.title: Sort the Questions
look.text: Four student questions about Exodus 3: (1) Did the burning bush really happen? (2) Why does Moses ask for God's name in 3:13, and what kind of answer does 3:14 give? (3) Is it wrong to send Moses back to Egypt? (4) Why does the text repeat "Moses, Moses" in 3:4, and where else does the Tanakh double a name?
look.prompt: Which questions does the text itself raise, and which do the students bring to it? Which could two careful readers answer differently by pointing at lines? Rewrite the weak ones.

check.q: Which passage size fits the capstone best?
choices: The whole book of Genesis
A short passage you can quote in full, roughly three to fifteen verses
One chapter from each part of the Tanakh
The entire Torah reading for one week
check.why: A capstone needs a passage short enough to quote and read closely; whole books cannot be argued line by line.

check.q: Which is a question the text raises rather than one the reader brings to it?
choices: Is God fair to Abraham?
Should people obey commands they find wrong?
Why does Genesis 22:2 give four descriptions of Isaac before naming him?
Did the binding of Isaac happen?
check.why: The four-step naming is something a plain reader notices in the verse; the others begin from the reader's own concerns.

check.q: Why does the course keep the capstone's stance descriptive?
choices: Because commentators never made claims
Because the Tanakh has no clear meaning
Because Rashi forbade arguments
Because a public-school class studies what a text does and how it has been read, not whether it is true
check.why: The descriptive frame is what allows academic study of a sacred text in a public school, following Abington v. Schempp.

lessons.title: Two Translations Side by Side
lessons.mainIdea: Reading your passage in JPS 1917 and one other translation shows where the Hebrew is hard, because that is where the translations differ.
reading: The course's text is the Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917. It is in the public domain, and it follows the traditional Hebrew text and its Jewish reading. Set beside it one other translation: the King James Version (1611), the American Standard Version (1901), or one to read but not quote: the New JPS (1985), Robert Alter (2004 for the Torah) or Everett Fox (1995). Where two translators agree, the Hebrew is probably plain. Where they differ, you have found a place where the Hebrew forces a choice, and that is a place to dig.

Take Genesis 22:2. JPS 1917 reads: "Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac." The KJV reads: "Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest." The KJV moves Isaac's name earlier, smoothing the sentence; JPS keeps the Hebrew order, in which the name comes last. That small difference is the whole point of Rashi's dialogue, which only works if the name is delayed. Fox, who tries to echo Hebrew rhythm, keeps the order too. A student who read only the KJV would never see the question.

Translation differences also reveal readings. Isaiah 7:14 has *almah*, which JPS 1917 renders "young woman" and the KJV "virgin," a choice that reflects the Christian reading of the verse through Matthew 1:23. Psalm 22:17 (22:16 in Christian numbering) has a disputed Hebrew word that JPS renders "like a lion" and the KJV "they pierced." Naming both renderings and the readers behind them, without ranking, is exactly the skill the capstone rewards. Always name the translation and its year when you quote.

words.d: the Jewish Publication Society's English Tanakh of 1917, public domain, the course's text
the English Bible of 1611, used in this course for comparison
the Hebrew word in Isaiah 7:14 that JPS renders "young woman" and the KJV "virgin"
the sequence of words in a sentence; Hebrew order often carries emphasis that translations change

look.title: The Name Comes Last
look.text: Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt-offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.
look.prompt: Read the verse aloud, then read it with "Isaac" moved to right after "son." What changes in how the command lands? Which order does the King James Version use, and why might a translator smooth it?

check.q: Why does a place where two translations differ deserve attention?
choices: It usually marks a place where the Hebrew forces a choice
It proves one translation is wrong
It shows the passage is not authentic
It means the verse is not in the Tanakh
check.why: Disagreement between careful translators points to a hard or ambiguous Hebrew phrase worth digging into.

check.q: How do JPS 1917 and the KJV differ at Genesis 22:2?
choices: JPS leaves out Moriah
The KJV moves Isaac's name earlier, while JPS keeps it last as in the Hebrew
The KJV calls Isaac a servant
JPS says "two sons"
check.why: JPS keeps the Hebrew order with the name delayed, which Rashi's dialogue depends on; the KJV smooths it.

check.q: Which translations may be quoted word for word in this course?
choices: Alter and Fox
The New JPS of 1985
JPS 1917, the KJV of 1611 and the ASV of 1901, which are public domain
Any translation printed after 1990
check.why: Only public-domain translations are quoted exactly; modern ones are read and paraphrased with the translator named.

lessons.title: Peshat: Structure and Key Words
lessons.mainIdea: Before any commentary, map the passage's structure and its repeated words, because that is where the text shows what it is doing.
reading: *Peshat* is the plain sense of the text: what the words say, in their order, in their context. Medieval commentators such as Rashbam and Ibn Ezra insisted on it first, and modern literary readers agree. Start by marking the passage's structure. Where does it begin and end? Who speaks, and how many times? Genesis 22 has three calls and three answers of "Here am I" (JPS 1917): to God in verse 1, to Isaac in verse 7, to the angel in verse 11. Noticing that pattern is peshat, and it already suggests a reading: the text organizes the story around Abraham answering.

Next, find the repeated words. Martin Buber and Franz Rosenzweig, translating the Tanakh into German in the 1920s, named this a *Leitwort*, a "leading word," one that recurs so as to carry meaning. In Genesis 22 the Hebrew for "son" appears again and again, and the word for "see" runs through the passage until the place is named "the LORD seeth" in verse 14. Robert Alter's The Art of Biblical Narrative (1981) made this method familiar to English readers. It works in a JPS translation with a pencil. Check the Hebrew word behind the English when you can.

Then read the passage's shape against its neighbors. Genesis 22 comes right after Abraham sends away Ishmael in chapter 21, so "thine only son" is loaded before God says it. A capstone that notices such context is doing what Ramban did constantly. It is also what Nechama Leibowitz (1905 to 1997), the great modern teacher of the weekly portion, trained a generation to do. Ask why this verse is here, and what changes if you imagine it gone.

words.d: the plain sense of a text: what the words say in their order and context
a "leading word" that repeats through a passage to carry its meaning; the term is Buber and Rosenzweig's
how a passage is built: its start and end, its speakers, its repeated patterns
a twentieth-century Israeli teacher whose worksheets taught close reading of the weekly portion with the commentators

look.title: Count the Answers
look.text: Genesis 22 (JPS 1917): verse 1, God calls "Abraham," and he says "Here am I." Verse 7, Isaac says "My father," and he says "Here am I, my son." Verse 11, the angel calls "Abraham, Abraham," and he says "Here am I." Three calls, three identical answers, to three different callers.
look.prompt: What does the repetition do to the reader's sense of Abraham? Why might the middle answer add "my son"? Write one sentence of peshat, with no commentary, about what the pattern shows.

check.q: What is peshat?
choices: The rabbinic method of filling gaps with stories
A translation of the Torah into German
A commentary by Rashi's grandson
The plain sense of the words in their order and context
check.why: Peshat is the plain sense; midrash fills gaps, and Rashbam is the grandson who wrote peshat commentary.

check.q: Who coined the term Leitwort, and what does it name?
choices: Buber and Rosenzweig; a leading word that repeats to carry meaning
Rashi; the first word of a parashah
Alter; a word the KJV mistranslates
Leibowitz; a worksheet question
check.why: Buber and Rosenzweig, translating in the 1920s, named the leading word; Alter later popularized the idea in English.

check.q: Why does Genesis 21 matter for reading "thine only son" in Genesis 22:2?
choices: Genesis 21 says Isaac is thirty-seven
Genesis 21 tells of Ishmael being sent away, so "only son" is already loaded
Genesis 21 names Moriah
Genesis 21 has no connection
check.why: Reading a passage against its neighbors is peshat; the sending away of Ishmael in chapter 21 shapes "only son."

lessons.title: Finding the Gaps
lessons.mainIdea: The Tanakh's narrative leaves out motives, ages and feelings, and every reader's interpretation begins in what the text does not say.
reading: Biblical narrative is spare. Erich Auerbach, in the first chapter of Mimesis (1946), compared Homer, who lights every detail, with Genesis 22, which tells nothing of the three days' walk, Abraham's face or Isaac's thoughts. Auerbach called the biblical style "fraught with background": everything is there, but withheld. Meir Sternberg's The Poetics of Biblical Narrative (1985) turned this into a method, reading gaps as places where the text makes the reader work. A capstone that names its passage's gaps has found where the arguments will be.

Genesis 4:8 is a famous gap. The JPS 1917 reads: "And Cain spoke unto Abel his brother. And it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him." Cain speaks, but the text never says what he said. The Samaritan Pentateuch and the ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, supply "Let us go into the field," and many scholars think words dropped out. Genesis Rabbah (22:7), a midrash collection of c. 400 to 500 CE, instead fills the silence with a quarrel: the brothers divided the world and each claimed the Temple site. Same gap, two kinds of filling: a textual repair and a story.

A gap is not a flaw to fix; it is the text's invitation. Some gaps are permanent: we are never told how old Isaac was, so Ibn Ezra's estimate and the midrash's thirty-seven are both guesses, and a careful student says so. Some are closed by the passage itself: verse 12 tells the reader what the test was for. List your passage's gaps in a column, and for each note whether the text ever closes it. That list is the raw material for the next section, where the commentators arrive.

words.d: something a narrative leaves unsaid, such as a motive, an age or a speech, that readers must fill or leave open
Erich Auerbach, whose Mimesis (1946) compared Homer's full detail with the withheld style of Genesis 22
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun c. 250 BCE, sometimes preserving different wording
a midrash collection on Genesis, c. 400-500 CE, that fills gaps with stories and verse-links

look.title: What Did Cain Say?
look.text: And Cain spoke unto Abel his brother. And it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.
look.prompt: Mark the exact spot where something is missing. Then compare two fillings: the Septuagint's "Let us go into the field" and Genesis Rabbah's quarrel over dividing the world. What does each filling assume about why the text is silent?

check.q: What did Auerbach mean by calling biblical narrative "fraught with background"?
choices: It has too many characters
It withholds details such as thoughts and settings, so much remains unspoken
It is longer than Homer
It always explains motives
check.why: Auerbach contrasted Homer's foreground detail with Genesis 22, where almost everything is left in the background.

check.q: How does Genesis Rabbah 22:7 fill the gap in Genesis 4:8?
choices: By adding the Greek phrase "Let us go into the field"
By saying Cain said nothing
By supplying a quarrel between the brothers
By moving the verse to chapter 5
check.why: The midrash supplies a story of a dispute; the Septuagint and Samaritan text supply a missing phrase instead.

check.q: Which statement about Isaac's age in Genesis 22 is the careful one?
choices: The text never gives it, so Ibn Ezra's guess and the midrash's thirty-seven are both readers' fillings
The text says thirty-seven
The text says thirteen
The KJV gives the age
check.why: Isaac's age is a permanent gap; both figures come from readers, not from the verse.

lessons.title: Rashi and the Midrash
lessons.mainIdea: Rashi reads for the plain sense but brings midrash wherever the text's gaps or oddities call for it, and he names which he is doing.
reading: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, *Rashi* (1040 to 1105), lived in Troyes in northern France. He wrote the commentary that Jewish readers have opened first for nine hundred years. He states his method at Genesis 3:8: he has come to give the plain sense and the aggadah that settles the words of Scripture. In practice that means he moves between *peshat* and *derash*, the interpretive filling, and a capstone should say which one he is using at your verse. On Genesis 22:2 he is using derash, borrowing the dialogue from Sanhedrin 89b and Genesis Rabbah 55.

Read Rashi as answering a question. On 22:2 the question is why four descriptions come before the name. His answer, in paraphrase, is that God gave the command slowly, to make it dear to Abraham and to reward him for each step. Notice what that reading assumes: that every extra word in the Torah is meaningful, that God speaks with intent, and that a delay is a kindness rather than a cruelty. A good capstone states the assumption, since it is the assumption, not the dialogue, that later commentators argue with.

On other verses Rashi is a strict peshat reader. On Genesis 22:12, "now I know that thou art a God-fearing man," he answers the obvious objection that God knew already. He reads "now I know" as "now I have an answer for those who ask." Whether or not a reader accepts the move, it shows Rashi doing what the capstone asks. He finds the difficulty, names it, and offers a reading that fits the words. Quote Rashi in paraphrase, cite the verse he is commenting on, and mark it "Rashi on Genesis 22:2."

words.d: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040-1105) of Troyes, France, whose commentary on the Tanakh is the one Jewish readers open first
interpretive reading that fills gaps and draws lessons, often through midrash; contrasted with peshat
the story and lesson side of rabbinic literature, as opposed to law
the Talmud page that gives the dialogue between God and Abraham over "thy son, thine only son"

look.title: Rashi Turns a Verse into a Dialogue
look.text: Rashi on Genesis 22:2, in paraphrase: Why does God not simply say "Isaac"? Because Abraham said, "I have two sons." God said, "Your only one." Abraham said, "Each is the only son of his mother." God said, "The one you love." Abraham said, "I love them both." So God said, "Isaac." And why the delay? So as not to shock him, and to give him reward for each word.
look.cite: Rashi, commentary on Genesis 22:2 (c. 1100), drawing on Talmud Sanhedrin 89b and Genesis Rabbah 55; paraphrased
look.prompt: What question about the verse is Rashi answering? What does his reading assume about how the Torah uses words? Could a peshat reader explain the four descriptions without a dialogue?

check.q: Where and when did Rashi live?
choices: Troyes, France, 1040-1105
Babylonia, c. 500 CE
Safed, the 1500s
check.why: Rashi lived in Troyes in northern France. Ibn Ezra was from Spain; the Safed mystics arranged Kabbalat Shabbat.

check.q: On Genesis 22:2, which method is Rashi using, and where does his reading come from?
choices: Peshat, from Ibn Ezra
Derash, from Sanhedrin 89b and Genesis Rabbah
Grammar, from the Masoretes
Allegory, from the Zohar
check.why: The dialogue is midrash, borrowed from the Talmud and Genesis Rabbah; Rashi marks such readings as derash.

check.q: What should a capstone state alongside Rashi's dialogue reading?
choices: That Rashi was wrong
That the KJV agrees
That the dialogue is in the Hebrew text
The assumption behind it, that every extra word in the Torah is meaningful
check.why: Naming the assumption is what lets a student show how later commentators argue with Rashi.

lessons.title: Ibn Ezra and Ramban Answer Back
lessons.mainIdea: Ibn Ezra and Ramban read the same verses with different tools, grammar and purpose, and often disagree with Rashi and each other.
reading: Abraham *Ibn Ezra* (1089 to c. 1164), born in Spain and a wanderer across Europe, wrote a commentary that is short, sharp and grammatical. He often dismisses a midrash as not the plain sense and then offers his own. On Genesis 22, he rejects the tradition that Isaac was thirty-seven with an argument from the text: if a grown man let himself be bound, his merit would be greater than his father's, and Scripture would have said so. He settles on about thirteen. Whether or not one agrees, it is a model of arguing from what the passage does and does not say.

Moses ben Nahman, *Ramban* (1194 to 1270), of Girona in Spain, wrote a commentary that constantly quotes Rashi and Ibn Ezra, agreeing, correcting, sometimes scolding. He also brings a layer neither of them has, hinting at kabbalah, the mystical reading, which he marks as secret. On Genesis 22:1, "God did prove Abraham," Ramban asks what a test can mean if God already knows. His answer, in paraphrase, is that a test is for the sake of the one tested. It brings a good that was only possible into action. So it earns a reward for a deed, not merely for a heart.

A capstone that uses both commentators shows a conversation across a century. Ibn Ezra asks what the words allow; Ramban asks what the event is for. Put them in your argument as voices, not as authorities: "Ibn Ezra objects that…" and "Ramban replies that…" Cite each as "Ibn Ezra on Genesis 22:4" or "Ramban on Genesis 22:1," in paraphrase. And keep a fourth voice, the midrash itself, since Genesis Rabbah 55 and 56 are the source both men are reacting to.

words.d: Abraham Ibn Ezra (1089-c. 1164), a Spanish-born grammarian and commentator who argued from the plain sense
Moses ben Nahman, Nahmanides (1194-1270), of Girona, whose commentary answers Rashi and Ibn Ezra and hints at kabbalah
Jewish mystical tradition, which Ramban brings into his commentary in hints
the word in Genesis 22:1 ("God did prove Abraham") whose meaning Ramban explains as for the sake of the one tested

look.title: Three Readers, One Silence
look.text: How old was Isaac in Genesis 22? Genesis Rabbah and later tradition: thirty-seven, since Sarah dies at the start of chapter 23 and a midrash links her death to the news. Ibn Ezra: about thirteen, because a grown man who accepted binding would be the story's hero, and the text says nothing of the kind. Ramban: focuses instead on the word "tested," asking what a test is for.
look.prompt: Which reader is arguing from what the text says, which from what it does not say, and which changes the question? Which move would you use in your own capstone, and why?

check.q: How does Ibn Ezra argue against the tradition that Isaac was thirty-seven?
choices: He quotes the KJV
He says the Septuagint gives Isaac's age
He argues that a grown man's willingness would have been the story's point, and the text says nothing of it
He says Sarah was already dead
check.why: Ibn Ezra reasons from the text's silence: if Isaac's merit were the greater, Scripture would have said so.

check.q: What does Ramban say a test is for, on Genesis 22:1?
choices: For the sake of the one tested, turning a possible good into a deed
To inform God of Abraham's heart
To punish Abraham for sending away Ishmael
To teach Isaac to obey
check.why: Ramban holds that God already knows; the test exists to bring Abraham's potential into action and earn reward for a deed.

check.q: How should the commentators appear in a capstone argument?
choices: As proofs that end the discussion
As voices in a conversation, each cited on the verse he comments on
As sources to quote word for word from modern translations
As one combined opinion called "the rabbis"
check.why: Ibn Ezra and Ramban disagree with Rashi and each other; the capstone treats them as distinct voices, cited by verse.

lessons.title: A Modern Reader at the Table
lessons.mainIdea: A twentieth- or twenty-first-century reader, literary, historical or feminist, adds a question the medieval commentators did not ask.
reading: The last voice in your capstone is a modern one. Literary readers such as Robert Alter and Meir Sternberg ask how the story is built and what its silences make the reader do. Historians and biblical scholars ask when a passage was written and what it meant in the ancient Near East. On Genesis 22, some connect it to laws against child sacrifice elsewhere in the Torah, such as Leviticus 18:21, while others, with Jon Levenson in The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son (1993), read it as a story about the transformation of an older idea. Neither claim is settled. A capstone reports both as scholars' proposals.

Feminist readers ask who is missing. Phyllis Trible, whose God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (1978) opened the field, and later readers note that Sarah never appears in Genesis 22. She dies at the start of chapter 23. They ask what the story looks like from her side. Midrash had already noticed the gap, which is why Genesis Rabbah connects her death to the news of the binding. Aviva Gottlieb Zornberg, in Genesis: The Beginning of Desire (1995), reads the midrash together with modern psychology and literature. Jewish and Christian readers, too, can be compared here. Christian tradition from the early church read Genesis 22 as prefiguring the crucifixion, a reading the capstone describes without ranking.

Pick one modern reader, read a few pages, and paraphrase carefully with the author, title and year. The point is not to declare that the modern reader is right and Rashi is wrong, or the reverse. It is to show what each reader's question lets them see. A rabbi in eleventh-century France, a grammarian in twelfth-century Spain and a professor in twentieth-century Berkeley each notice something the others did not, and the passage is large enough to hold all of them.

words.d: reading the Tanakh for how its stories are built: structure, repetition, point of view, gaps
a biblical scholar whose 1978 book opened feminist reading of the Hebrew Bible
in Christian reading, an earlier event understood as a pattern of a later one; the church read Genesis 22 as prefiguring the crucifixion
Aviva Gottlieb Zornberg, whose Genesis: The Beginning of Desire (1995) reads midrash with modern literature and psychology

look.title: Where Is Sarah?
look.text: Genesis 22 never mentions Sarah. Genesis 23:1-2 opens with her death. Genesis Rabbah connects the two, telling that the news of the binding was what killed her. A feminist reader asks: what does the story look like from Sarah's side, and why does the text keep her out? A literary reader asks: what does her absence do to the reader's experience of chapter 22?
look.prompt: The midrash and the modern reader notice the same gap. How do their responses differ? What question could you ask about Sarah that stays with the text and does not become a verdict on the tradition?

check.q: What kind of question does a literary reader like Sternberg bring to Genesis 22?
choices: When was the passage written?
How is the story built, and what do its silences make the reader do?
Is the story true?
What did Rashi say?
check.why: Literary criticism asks about structure, repetition and gaps; dating is the historian's question.

check.q: Which observation is shared by Genesis Rabbah and feminist readers?
choices: That Isaac was thirty-seven
That Moriah is Jerusalem
That Sarah is absent from Genesis 22 and dies at the start of chapter 23
That Abraham had only one son
check.why: Both the midrash and modern feminist readers notice Sarah's absence, though they respond to it differently.

check.q: How should a capstone present the Christian reading of Genesis 22 as prefiguring the crucifixion?
choices: As the correct reading
As a mistake to be corrected
As a reading that proves the Jewish one wrong
As a described reading of that tradition, set beside Jewish readings without ranking
check.why: The course describes each tradition's readings without judging which is true.

lessons.title: A Thesis About What the Text Does
lessons.mainIdea: A capstone thesis claims something about what the passage does with its words and how readers have responded, and it can be shown from the text.
reading: A thesis is one sentence that a reader could disagree with and that the rest of your paper defends. Weak thesis: "Genesis 22 is a powerful story about faith." No one can disagree, and it points to no line. Stronger: "Genesis 22:2 delays Isaac's name to make the reader feel the weight of the command, and Rashi's dialogue, Ibn Ezra's question about age and Auerbach's 'background' are three ways of filling the same pause." That sentence names a feature of the text, a claim about its effect, and a claim about its readers, and each part can be checked.

Build the thesis from your peshat notes and your gap list. The pattern is usually: the text does X (structure, key word, gap); the effect on a reader is Y; readers A, B and C respond to X in ways that show Z. Keep the verbs about the text: delays, repeats, withholds, frames, echoes. Avoid verbs about truth: proves, reveals, shows that God. This is the same discipline as the course's voice: "the text says," "Rashi reads," "scholars propose."

Then outline. A clear capstone has an opening that quotes the passage in JPS 1917 and states the thesis. A peshat section on structure, key words and gaps. A section on the commentators, each cited on the verse. A section on a modern reader. A section that names other readings and what they see. And a closing that says what the argument leaves open. The Talmud's teachers argued this way, too: Pirkei Avot (5:22 in most editions) reports Ben Bag Bag's saying, in paraphrase, to turn the Torah over and over, for everything is in it. A thesis is one turn.

words.d: a one-sentence claim that a reader could dispute and the paper defends from the text
a statement that needs support; in this course, about what a text does or how a reader read it
a sage quoted in Pirkei Avot for the saying that one should turn the Torah over and over, since everything is in it

look.title: Fix the Thesis
look.text: Three draft theses on Jonah 4: (A) "Jonah is a story about learning mercy." (B) "The book of Jonah proves that God cares about Nineveh." (C) "Jonah 4 ends on an unanswered question (4:11), and by leaving Jonah's reply out, the text hands the question to the reader; the rabbis' choice to read Jonah on Yom Kippur afternoon shows they took that handoff seriously."
look.prompt: Which thesis can be disagreed with and checked against lines? Which one asserts something about God rather than about the text? Rewrite A and B so they make claims about what the text does.

check.q: Which thesis is strongest for a capstone?
choices: "Genesis 22:2 delays Isaac's name to make the reader feel the command's weight, and three readers fill that pause differently"
"Genesis 22 is a powerful story about faith"
"Genesis 22 proves Abraham was right"
"Genesis 22 is in the Torah"
check.why: It names a feature of the text, an effect and a claim about readers, each of which can be checked; the others cannot be disputed or make truth claims.

check.q: Which verbs belong in a capstone thesis about the Tanakh?
choices: proves, reveals, shows that God
delays, repeats, withholds, frames, echoes
believes, worships, obeys
is true, is false, is history
check.why: Verbs about what the text does keep the thesis descriptive; verbs about truth take a side the course does not take.

check.q: What does the saying attributed to Ben Bag Bag in Pirkei Avot add to the idea of a thesis?
choices: That only one reading is correct
That the Torah should not be studied
That a thesis is one turn of a text that can be turned again and again
That Avot was written by Rashi
check.why: "Turn it over and over" pictures the text as inexhaustible; a thesis is one honest turn, not the last word.

lessons.title: Citing Book, Verse and Commentator
lessons.mainIdea: Every claim in a capstone points to a place: book, chapter and verse for the text, the verse commented on for a commentator, and the translation and year for a quotation.
reading: Citation in this course is simple and strict. For the Tanakh, give book, chapter and verse: Genesis 22:2. Note that Jewish and Christian chapter numbering sometimes differs; Psalm 22:17 in JPS 1917 is 22:16 in the KJV, because JPS counts the heading as verse 1. When you quote, name the translation and year: "(Genesis 22:2, JPS 1917)." When you paraphrase a modern translation such as Alter or Fox, say so: "Fox renders the phrase as roughly…" Do not quote modern translations at length; they are under copyright, and the course's rule is public-domain quotations only.

For a commentator, cite the verse he is commenting on, not a page: "Rashi on Genesis 22:2," "Ibn Ezra on Genesis 22:4," "Ramban on Genesis 22:1." For midrash, give the collection and section: "Genesis Rabbah 55:7." For the Talmud, give the tractate and page with side: "Sanhedrin 89b." For Pirkei Avot, chapter and mishnah: "Avot 5:22." For a modern book, author, title and year: "Alter, The Art of Biblical Narrative, 1981." Everything you cite must exist and say what you say it says. If you cannot check it, leave it out; that is the same rule this course has followed on every page.

Citations do a second job: they attribute. "Isaac was thirteen" is a claim you cannot support. "Ibn Ezra, on Genesis 22:4, argues that Isaac was about thirteen" is a fact about a reader, which you can. Attribution is how a paper on a sacred text stays honest in a public school: every belief has a believer, every reading a reader, and the student stands outside describing them. That is not a weaker position than arguing for a belief; it is a different, and harder, discipline.

words.d: the exact place a claim points to: book, chapter and verse; commentator on a verse; tractate and page; author, title and year
naming whose reading or belief a statement is, so the paper describes readers instead of asserting their claims
one of the books of the Talmud, such as Sanhedrin or Berakhot, cited by page and side (89b)
the count of verses in a chapter, which differs in some psalms between Jewish and Christian Bibles

look.title: Dates Behind the Citations
rows: Alter, The Art of Biblical Narrative
look.cite: Standard reference dates; approximate dates rounded
look.prompt: How many centuries separate the midrash from Rashi, and Rashi from Alter? What does that span suggest about the phrase "a conversation across time"?

check.q: How should a student cite Rashi's reading of the four descriptions of Isaac?
choices: "Rashi, page 22"
"Rashi on Genesis 22:2"
"Rashi, Talmud 1105"
"Rashi, JPS 1917"
check.why: Commentators are cited by the verse they comment on; JPS 1917 is a translation, not a commentary.

check.q: Why do Psalm 22:17 (JPS) and Psalm 22:16 (KJV) point to the same line?
choices: The KJV skipped a verse
JPS added a verse
JPS counts the psalm's heading as verse 1, so its numbers run one higher
They are different psalms
check.why: Jewish editions number the heading as verse 1 in many psalms, so JPS numbers are often one higher than the KJV's.

check.q: What is the difference between "Isaac was thirteen" and "Ibn Ezra argues that Isaac was about thirteen"?
choices: The first is a claim about the text that cannot be supported; the second is an attributed fact about a reader
The first is Hebrew and the second is English
There is no difference
The second is a quotation and the first is a paraphrase
check.why: Attribution turns an unsupported claim into a checkable statement about what a reader said.

lessons.title: Other Readings, Honestly Named
lessons.mainIdea: A strong argument states the best other readings fairly and explains what they see, rather than hiding them.
reading: The rabbis built disagreement into their texts. The Mishnah records minority views by name. The Talmud in Eruvin 13b tells that after years of dispute between the schools of Hillel and Shammai, a heavenly voice declared, in paraphrase, that both are the words of the living God, and that the law follows Hillel because his school was humble and taught Shammai's view before its own. Whatever one makes of the voice, the practice is clear: state the other side first, and state it well. The printed *Mikraot Gedolot* page does the same, setting Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ramban around the verse so a reader sees them argue.

In a capstone, a section on other readings does three things. It names a reading that differs from your thesis, in its own strongest form. It shows what that reading sees in the text that yours does not. And it explains why you still hold your thesis, or how your thesis changes to take the other reading in. If Rosa's thesis is that the delayed name makes the reader feel the weight, the best other reading is Rashi's: the delay is a kindness to Abraham, not a pressure on the reader. Rosa has to say what Rashi's reading explains that hers does not.

The most famous rabbinic story about disagreement is the oven of Akhnai in Bava Metzia 59b. Rabbi Eliezer calls on miracles and a heavenly voice to prove his ruling. Rabbi Joshua answers with Deuteronomy 30:12, "It is not in heaven," and the majority's reading stands. Readers have taken the story in many directions, from a charter for human interpretation to a warning about how the majority treated Eliezer afterward. For the capstone the lesson is modest: a reading is defended with the text and the argument, not with authority, and the losing side is still recorded by name.

words.d: the "great Scriptures," the printed Bible page with the verse surrounded by Targum and several commentaries
the Talmud page reporting that both Hillel's and Shammai's views are "the words of the living God"
the story in Bava Metzia 59b in which the majority's reading stands against a heavenly voice, citing "It is not in heaven"
a reading that differs from your thesis, stated in its strongest form before you answer it

look.title: Not in Heaven
look.text: It is not in heaven, that thou shouldest say: 'Who shall go up for us to heaven, and bring it unto us, and make us to hear it, that we may do it?'
look.cite: Deuteronomy 30:12, Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917; cited by Rabbi Joshua in Talmud Bava Metzia 59b
look.prompt: In Deuteronomy the verse says the commandment is near and doable. How does Rabbi Joshua reuse it in the Talmud's story? Is that a peshat reading or a derash reading, and does that matter for the point he makes?

check.q: What does the Talmud in Eruvin 13b say about the disputes of Hillel and Shammai?
choices: That Shammai's school was always right
That both schools spoke the words of the living God, and the law follows Hillel
That the disputes were forbidden
That a majority vote settled them in Rashi's time
check.why: Eruvin 13b records the heavenly voice affirming both and gives Hillel's humility as the reason the law follows his school.

check.q: What should a section on other readings do first?
choices: Explain why the other reading is foolish
Skip to the conclusion
Ignore any reading by a commentator
State the strongest form of a reading that differs from the thesis
check.why: The rabbinic practice, and the capstone's, is to state the other side well before answering it.

check.q: In the oven of Akhnai story, what verse does Rabbi Joshua cite, and to what effect?
choices: Genesis 22:2, to prove the oven pure
Psalm 19:9, to end the debate
Deuteronomy 30:12, "It is not in heaven," so the majority's reading stands over a heavenly voice
Exodus 15:1, to celebrate a victory
check.why: Rabbi Joshua's citation of Deuteronomy 30:12 is the story's turning point; the majority's interpretation prevails.

lessons.title: Chavruta: Arguing in Pairs
lessons.mainIdea: Presenting the capstone in chavruta, a study pair, follows the traditional Jewish way of learning by argument with a partner.
reading: Jewish study has long been done in pairs. The word *chavruta* comes from the Aramaic for "friend" or "companion," and it names both the partner and the method. Two people read a text aloud, question each other and argue until each can state the other's view. Pirkei Avot 1:6 records the advice, in paraphrase, to get yourself a teacher and acquire a companion. The Talmud in Ta'anit 7a reads Proverbs 27:17, "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" (JPS 1917), as a picture of scholars sharpening each other. Walk into a *beit midrash*, a study hall, today and the sound is not silence but a hundred arguments.

The capstone presentation borrows this form. Two students who worked on related passages sit facing each other, with the class around them. One states a thesis and reads the key lines. The other does not applaud; the other pushes: which word carries that? what does Ramban say against you? what would a feminist reader notice? Then they switch. The class's job is to write down the strongest question asked and the best answer given. A presentation is judged partly on how well a student states the partner's reading back, since that is what chavruta trains.

Rules keep it kind. Every challenge points to a line. Nobody speaks about a tradition's truth, only about its readings. Nobody is stuck defending a thesis that the argument has improved; changing your claim in the middle, and saying why, is a win. Dev and Rosa in the opening story did exactly that, and they ended with a shared question instead of two separate answers. That ending is the point of the form: the text got read more closely than either of them could have managed alone.

words.d: a study partner, and the method of learning a text by reading and arguing in pairs; from the Aramaic for "friend"
"house of study," a hall where texts are studied aloud in pairs and groups
the Talmud page that reads Proverbs 27:17, "iron sharpeneth iron," as scholars sharpening each other

look.title: Iron on Iron
look.text: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
look.cite: Proverbs 27:17, Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917; read in Talmud Ta'anit 7a as about study partners
look.prompt: What does the image of iron on iron say about how a good study partner treats you? What kind of question sharpens, and what kind only cuts?

check.q: What does chavruta mean and name?
choices: A study partner and the method of learning by argument in pairs
The lecture given by a rabbi
A written commentary on the Talmud
The chant for reading Torah
check.why: Chavruta, from the Aramaic for friend, names both the partner and the paired method of study.

check.q: Which verse does Ta'anit 7a read as being about scholars sharpening each other?
choices: Deuteronomy 6:4
Genesis 22:2
Proverbs 27:17
Psalm 145:16
check.why: "Iron sharpeneth iron" from Proverbs 27:17 is read in the Talmud as a picture of study partners.

check.q: In the capstone presentation, what counts as a win for the presenter?
choices: Never changing the thesis
Getting the partner to agree
Speaking longest
Stating the partner's reading fairly and improving the thesis when the argument calls for it
check.why: Chavruta trains a student to hold the other view accurately; a thesis improved mid-argument is a success, not a loss.

lessons.title: The Rubric and the Reflection
lessons.mainIdea: The capstone is scored on reading, attribution and argument, and it closes with a reflection on what it means to study a sacred text in a public school.
reading: The rubric rewards the moves this chapter has taught. Close reading of the passage in two translations, with structure, key words and gaps named. Commentators used as distinct voices, cited on the verse. A modern reader paraphrased with author, title and year. A thesis about what the text does, defended from lines. Other readings stated fairly. Every belief attributed, every source real. And a presentation in which the student can state a partner's reading back. Style counts less than accuracy: a plain sentence that cites a verse beats a grand one that does not.

The final page is a reflection, and it asks a question the course has carried since its first chapter. This is a public school in Illinois. The Supreme Court said in Abington v. Schempp (1963) that the Bible may be studied "objectively as part of a secular program of education," and Justice Clark's opinion added that one's education is not complete without a study of religion. That sentence set the frame: describe, attribute, compare, and never tell a classmate what to believe. Write about what that frame made possible and what it made hard. Was there a moment when describing a reading felt different from holding it? Did any reader, Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Trible, Alter, make you see the text in a way you did not expect?

Some students in the room hold the Tanakh as Scripture. Some hold other Scriptures. Some hold none. The course has asked all of them to read the same verse with the same care and to say "the text says" and "Rashi reads" in the same voice. Jewish tradition has a phrase for study done for its own sake, *Torah lishmah*, and the rabbis praised it above study for reward. A public-school course cannot ask for that in a religious sense. It can ask for something near it: reading a text well because it is there, because people have loved and argued over it for millennia, and because learning to describe a belief you may not share is one of the best things a school can teach.

words.d: the list of criteria and points by which the capstone is scored
a short closing piece in which the student looks back on what studying the text taught them
"Torah for its own sake," study done for the study itself, which the rabbis praised
the Supreme Court's phrase in Abington v. Schempp (1963) for the setting in which the Bible may be studied objectively in public schools

look.title: Capstone Rubric
rows: Close reading in two translations: structure, key words, gaps
Commentators as distinct voices, cited on the verse
A modern reader, paraphrased with author, title, year
Thesis about what the text does, defended from lines
Chavruta presentation and stating the partner's view
look.cite: Course rubric for the Tanakh capstone, Architecture of Grace
look.prompt: Which three criteria carry most of the weight, and why do you think the course put it there? Where would a beautifully written paper with no citations lose the most?

check.q: What did Justice Clark's opinion in Abington v. Schempp (1963) add beyond permitting objective study of the Bible?
choices: That the KJV must be used
That one's education is not complete without a study of religion
That only Jewish students may study the Tanakh
That public schools must hold prayer
check.why: Schempp barred devotional exercises but stated that education is incomplete without the study of religion, presented objectively.

check.q: According to the rubric, which matters more in a capstone: elegant style or accurate citation?
choices: Style, because the rubric scores writing
Neither is scored
Accurate citation, since attribution and real sources are scored and style counts less
Style, because Rashi wrote beautifully
check.why: The rubric weights close reading, attribution and argument; a plain cited sentence beats a grand uncited one.

check.q: What does Torah lishmah mean, and how does the lesson relate it to a public school?
choices: "Torah for its own sake"; the school cannot ask for it religiously but can ask for careful reading for its own sake
"Torah in Hebrew"; the school must teach Hebrew
"Torah in the home"; the school sends work home
"Torah for reward"; the school gives grades
check.why: Torah lishmah is study for its own sake; the course asks for its secular neighbor, reading a text well because it is there.

review.q: Which order of steps matches the capstone method?
choices: Modern reader, thesis, then find a passage
Passage and question, two translations, peshat and gaps, commentators, modern reader, thesis, other readings
Thesis first, then look for verses that agree
Commentators first, then the text
review.why: The capstone reads plainly first, then hears the commentators and a modern reader, then argues.

review.q: Why does Rashi's dialogue reading of Genesis 22:2 depend on the translation's word order?
choices: Because it only works if Isaac's name comes last, as in the Hebrew and JPS 1917
Because the KJV includes the dialogue
Because Rashi wrote in English
Because the dialogue is in Genesis 21
review.why: The delay of the name is what Rashi explains; the KJV moves the name earlier and hides the question.

review.q: Which reader argued from the text's silence that Isaac could not have been thirty-seven?
choices: Rashi
Ramban
Ibn Ezra
Auerbach
review.why: Ibn Ezra reasoned that a grown Isaac's merit would have been named; Ramban focused on the meaning of the test.

review.q: What is a gap, in the sense this chapter uses?
choices: A verse missing from the Dead Sea Scrolls
A chapter break added by Christians
A blank space in a Torah scroll
Something the narrative leaves unsaid, such as a motive, an age or a speech
review.why: Gaps are the narrative's silences; Genesis 4:8, where Cain's words are missing, is the chapter's example.

choices: "Ramban on Genesis 22:1"
"Ramban, page 89b"
"Genesis Rabbah, JPS 1917"
"Sanhedrin, chapter 22"
review.why: Commentators are cited on the verse; midrash by collection and section; Talmud by tractate and page with side.

review.q: What does Eruvin 13b's "these and these are the words of the living God" model for a capstone?
choices: That the student should never take a position
That the other reading is stated fairly and recorded even when one view is followed
That Shammai's view is always ignored
That a heavenly voice decides arguments
review.why: The passage affirms both schools and still follows one; the capstone states counter-readings well before answering them.

review.q: In a chavruta presentation, what is the partner's job?
choices: To agree and summarize
To grade the paper
To read the passage in Hebrew
To push with questions that point to lines and to test the thesis
review.why: Chavruta is learning by argument; the partner sharpens the thesis, as Ta'anit 7a reads Proverbs 27:17.

review.q: Which sentence keeps the course's stance?
choices: "Genesis 22 proves Abraham's faith was rewarded by God."
"The Christian reading is a misreading of the Tanakh."
"Ramban reads the test in Genesis 22:1 as existing for the sake of the one tested."
"The binding of Isaac never happened."
review.why: Only the third describes a reader's reading; the others assert or deny a tradition's truth or a historical claim.
